script.opening: (You play the daughter, Lisa, with Harold beside you.) "We're a bit worried about Dad — over the last few weeks he's gone more confused and forgetful, he's really constipated, his mouth's bone dry, his vision's blurry, and ironically his waterworks are WORSE — he can barely go. Is this just his age catching up? Or… is he getting dementia? It came on quite quickly, which is what's scared us."

facts.text: If asked: three weeks ago the practice started a bladder tablet (oxybutynin) because he was rushing to the toilet. Within a week he was "foggy". Before that he did his own crossword, managed his money and drove to the shops.
Forgetting conversations, muddled about the day, once put the kettle in the fridge. Worse in the evenings. No falls, no head injury, no fever.
"I keep feeling I need to go but only a dribble comes out." Last passed a small amount about two hours ago. Lower tummy feels "full and a bit sore". No blood, no burning.
Mouth very dry, has to sip water constantly. Reading glasses "don't work any more". Bowels open every four or five days, hard. Heart sometimes "racing".

facts.topic: Medicines (if asked for the full list)
facts.text: Oxybutynin, amitriptyline 25 mg at night "for years, for my back", and paracetamol.

facts.topic: Over-the-counter — only if asked about anything bought from the chemist or supermarket
facts.text: Harold, sheepishly: "I take a couple of those Nytol sleeping tablets most nights." Lisa did not know.
Harold, 78, retired engineer, widowed, lives alone, Lisa visits daily. Mild prostate symptoms for years. No allergies. No diagnosis of dementia.
Your mum had Alzheimer's and you nursed her for five years. You are terrified it is starting with Dad. Say this only if asked what worries you most.

Lisa is anxious and does most of the talking; Harold is a bit vague and embarrassed. If the doctor asks Harold directly, he answers simply. If the doctor explains this could well be the tablets and is likely to improve once they are stopped, Lisa is visibly relieved and may cry: "I thought we were losing him." Ask: "Should he stop them all today?"

ice.concerns: Lisa (only if asked): "I nursed Mum through Alzheimer's — I can't bear it happening to Dad."
ice.expectations: An explanation and to know whether this can get better.

cues: "It came on quite quickly." — say in the opening.
"His waterworks are worse, not better." — say in the opening.
Harold: "I only take something from the chemist to help me sleep." — say only if asked about non-prescribed medicines.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the symptom cluster (confusion, constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary RETENTION) coming on after a new ANTIMUSCARINIC as ANTICHOLINERGIC TOXICITY / high anticholinergic burden — a reversible IATROGENIC cause — rather than accepting "ageing" or "dementia"

Takes a full MEDICATION history INCLUDING OTC/self-bought items, and identifies the STACKED anticholinergics: oxybutynin + amitriptyline + the sedating antihistamine (and recognises oxybutynin given for urgency has caused retention)

Plans DEPRESCRIBING: stop/reduce the culprit anticholinergics (stop oxybutynin; review/taper amitriptyline — not recommended for low back pain by NICE NG59 — and stop the antihistamine) and consider safer alternatives for the urinary urgency, the back pain, and sleep — reducing the anticholinergic burden

Assesses the URINARY RETENTION — over video by history (pain, dribbling/overflow, time since he last passed urine, lower abdominal swelling), arranging a same-day face-to-face examination for a palpable bladder and a bladder scan/residual volume (degree, acute vs chronic) and acts on it appropriately — recognising acute retention may need urgent assessment/catheterisation — and rechecks cognition once off the drugs, expecting improvement

Avoids the prescribing cascade: does NOT add further drugs or label dementia for what is an iatrogenic, reversible picture; plans to reassess cognition formally only after withdrawing the culprits if concern persists

Surfaces and addresses the daughter’s unspoken DEMENTIA fear, delivering the hopeful reframe (this is likely a reversible medication effect, not dementia) with compassion; handles the OTC-medication disclosure non-judgementally
Engages the patient and daughter as partners, validates that the rapid onset rightly worried them, and explains the plan clearly

Safety-nets and follows up: the deprescribing plan and safer alternatives, retention assessment and red flags (complete inability to pass urine/severe pain → urgent), a recheck of cognition/symptoms after withdrawal expecting improvement, and a review — reversing the iatrogenic harm rather than compounding it

worked.txt: "I can see you’re both frightened this is dementia — so let me give you some genuinely reassuring news first. The fact this came on quite quickly, over a few weeks, and right after a new tablet was started, points away from dementia and towards something we can REVERSE: the medicines themselves."

"There’s a group of medicines that, especially when you take several together, can cause exactly this combination — muddled thinking, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and trouble passing urine. The new bladder tablet, oxybutynin, is one; the old amitriptyline for your back is another. Can I ask — are you taking anything for sleep from the chemist? … An antihistamine. That’s a third one. Together they’ve tipped you over."

"Here’s the cruel irony: the bladder tablet you were given to help your waterworks has actually made you unable to wee properly — that’s the same family of effects. So adding MORE tablets would be the wrong direction; the fix is taking some AWAY."

"So my plan is to stop the oxybutynin, and review and most likely stop the amitriptyline and the sleep antihistamine, and find gentler alternatives for your bladder, your back and your sleep. I’d expect the confusion, the dry mouth and the constipation to lift, and your waterworks to ease, over the next couple of weeks."

"One thing I do need to check today — how your bladder is right now. I can’t examine your tummy over video, so I’d like to see you in person today to check it and scan your bladder, because if it’s very full and you really can’t go, that sometimes needs sorting urgently. If at any point you completely can’t pass urine and your tummy’s painful and swollen, that’s an emergency — go to A&E."

"We’ll stop the culprits, sort safer options, and I’ll see Dad again in a couple of weeks — I’m expecting a real improvement. IF, once he’s off these, there’s still a memory concern, then we’d look into that properly — but I think you’ll have your dad back. You were right to bring him; the quick onset was the clue, and it’s a fixable one."

f.learning: A cluster of new/worsening confusion, constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision and urinary RETENTION coming on over weeks after starting an ANTIMUSCARINIC — on top of other anticholinergics (amitriptyline, a sedating antihistamine) — is ANTICHOLINERGIC TOXICITY / high anticholinergic burden: a reversible IATROGENIC mimic, not "ageing" or new dementia, with the rapid onset linked to a medication change as the giveaway. There is a cruel irony to spot: the oxybutynin given FOR urinary urgency has caused retention. The task is a full medication review INCLUDING OTC items, identifying the stacked anticholinergics and DEPRESCRIBING them (stop oxybutynin; review and taper amitriptyline, which NICE NG59 does not recommend for low back pain; stop the antihistamine; safer alternatives for the urgency, back pain and sleep), assessing the urinary retention (acute retention may need urgent action), and rechecking cognition once off the drugs — avoiding the prescribing cascade of adding more drugs or labelling dementia. The examinable hidden agenda is the family’s unspoken dementia terror; deliver the hopeful, evidence-based reframe (likely reversible, not dementia), handle the OTC disclosure non-judgementally, and follow up to confirm improvement — reversing iatrogenic harm rather than compounding it.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG97 — Dementia (2018): medicines with anticholinergic burden · NICE CG97 — Lower urinary tract symptoms in men (2010, updated 2015)
knowledge.summary: New confusion, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation and difficulty passing urine weeks after starting oxybutynin — on top of amitriptyline and a bought sedating antihistamine — is anticholinergic burden until proven otherwise. Reduce the burden, check for retention today, and reassess memory only once the drugs are out.

points.t: Anticholinergic effects: confusion and memory problems, drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, fast heart rate. Several drugs together add up; older people are most sensitive. Onset over weeks after a new drug points to the drug, not dementia.

Be aware that some commonly prescribed medicines add to anticholinergic burden and cause cognitive impairment. Consider minimising them, and look for alternatives, when assessing whether to refer someone with suspected dementia. Validated burden scales exist; NICE NG97 does not favour one.

Sedating antihistamines sold for sleep are anticholinergic and are often not on the GP record. A full medicine review includes over-the-counter and herbal products (NICE NG5, medicines optimisation, 2015).

Stop the oxybutynin and the bought antihistamine. Amitriptyline should be withdrawn gradually rather than stopped abruptly (BNF); NICE NG59 does not recommend tricyclics for low back pain, so review its purpose. STOPP/START (version 3, 2023, international) lists these combinations in older adults.

Anticholinergics can cause urinary retention — palpable bladder, pain, dribbling or overflow. Acute painful retention needs same-day catheterisation. Subacute confusion also needs a delirium check (NICE CG103): look for infection, constipation, retention, dehydration and check bloods including U&E.

For men with overactive bladder symptoms, NICE CG97 advises bladder training and assessment of the lower urinary tract (including residual volume) before drugs. If a drug is needed, mirabegron is an option (NICE TA290); it is contraindicated in severe uncontrolled hypertension, so check BP (MHRA Drug Safety Update, October 2015).

Impact on daily life, falls, the family’s fear of care homes, how he manages at home.

Anticholinergic burden versus delirium from infection or retention, versus a new dementia.
Acute urinary retention, delirium, renal impairment from obstruction.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

Reviews why amitriptyline is prescribed (NICE NG59), sleep and back pain alternatives, constipation.
A&E for complete retention or pain; delirium symptoms named; review in about two weeks; Yellow Card report.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Followed “it came on quickly” and “opposite of what I went for”; picked up the hesitation before the OTC disclosure.
Idea (age or dementia); concern (losing him, care homes); expectation (an explanation and maybe a memory test).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Lisa (only if asked): "I nursed Mum through Alzheimer's — I can't bear it happening to Dad." — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, Mr Inglis — I’m Dr Lee. Can you both see and hear me all right? And Mr Inglis, are you happy for your daughter to be part of this conversation?
model.why: Checks the video link and seeks the patient’s own consent for a third party

model.text: (Harold) Yes, yes, she’s fine to stay. (Daughter) We’re worried about Dad. Over the last few weeks he’s got confused and forgetful, really constipated, his mouth’s bone dry, his vision’s blurry — and his waterworks are worse, he can barely go. Is this his age, or is he getting dementia? It came on so quickly.
Thank you, that’s a really clear description. I can hear that the word dementia is on your mind — we will come back to it, I promise. First, Mr Inglis, how do you feel things are?
model.why: Acknowledges the dementia fear and brings the patient in directly

model.text: (Harold) Muddled, doctor. And I can’t pass water properly. It’s the opposite of what I went to the doctor for.
That’s an important clue. When did all this start — before or after the new bladder tablet?
model.why: Links timing of symptoms to the medication change

model.text: (Daughter) After. It was about three weeks ago he started the new one, and it’s been downhill since.
Right now, Mr Inglis — are you able to pass any urine at all? Any pain or swelling low in your tummy?
(Harold) A bit, in dribbles. It feels full, uncomfortable, but not agony.
Thank you. Any fever, being sick, falls, or times in the day when you’re much more confused than others?
model.why: Screens for infection, falls and fluctuating delirium

model.text: (Daughter) No fever. He’s been a bit worse some evenings, but no falls.

Now I’d like to go through every tablet. I can see the oxybutynin and the amitriptyline on the record. Are there any others — anything from the chemist or the supermarket, for sleep, colds or allergies?
model.why: Takes a full medication history including over-the-counter items

model.text: (Harold, after a pause) Well… I take a sleeping tablet from the chemist. An antihistamine one. I didn’t think it counted.
I’m really glad you mentioned it — lots of people don’t realise those count, and it’s actually very helpful.
model.why: Responds to the disclosure without judgement

model.text: (To the daughter) You mentioned dementia. What’s been going through your mind?
(Daughter) That we’re losing him. That this is the start of it and it only goes one way.
That’s a frightening thought, and it makes sense you’d worry. What were you both hoping I could do today?
(Daughter) Just to know what it is. And whether he needs a memory test.

Then here’s some genuinely hopeful news. Dementia usually creeps in over months or years. This came on over weeks, right after a new tablet. There’s a family of medicines that, especially when you take several together, cause exactly this: muddled thinking, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation and trouble passing urine. The bladder tablet is one. The amitriptyline is another. And the chemist sleeping tablet is a third.
model.why: Names anticholinergic burden as the likely reversible cause

model.text: (Harold) So the tablet for my bladder has stopped my bladder working?

That’s exactly it — it’s a known side effect, and it’s why adding more tablets would be the wrong direction. The fix is taking some away. I can’t promise, but I’d expect a real improvement over the next couple of weeks once they’re out of your system.
model.why: Honest, hopeful reframe that answers the dementia fear

model.text: (Daughter) Oh, thank goodness. I’d already been reading about care homes.

Here’s what I suggest. Stop the oxybutynin today, and stop the chemist sleeping tablet. The amitriptyline needs to come down gradually rather than stopping suddenly — I’ll give you a simple plan. Does that sound all right to you, Mr Inglis?
model.why: Deprescribing plan with safe amitriptyline withdrawal, agreed with the patient

model.text: (Harold) Yes. I want my head back.

There’s one thing I can’t do on video: feel your bladder. Because it feels full and you’re only dribbling, I want you seen in person today for an examination and a bladder scan, and some blood tests including your kidneys. If your bladder is holding a lot, you may need a catheter for a while to let it recover.
model.why: Arranges same-day face-to-face retention assessment and bloods

model.text: (Daughter) I can bring him in this afternoon.

Thank you. For the urgency, once things settle, we’ll try bladder training first and look at other options that don’t affect thinking. For sleep and your back, we’ll find gentler approaches rather than more tablets. And I’ll report this reaction so it’s recorded.
model.why: Plans safer alternatives and Yellow Card reporting

model.text: (Harold) That’s a relief.

Before you come in — if you can’t pass any urine at all, or the tummy becomes painful and swollen, go straight to A&E. Same if you become very drowsy, feverish or suddenly much more confused. I’ll see you again in about two weeks to check your memory and thinking once these medicines are out. If there’s still a concern then, we’ll look into it properly.
model.why: Specific retention and delirium safety-net; planned cognitive reassessment

model.text: (Daughter) Okay. That’s clear.
Could one of you tell me back which tablets are stopping and what happens this afternoon?
(Daughter) Stop the bladder tablet and the chemist sleeping one, cut the amitriptyline down slowly, come in this afternoon for the bladder check and bloods, and back in two weeks.
Perfect. You were right to bring him — the speed it came on was the clue, and it’s a fixable one.
model.why: Affirms the family’s concern and closes warmly

social.t: Sudden confusion threatens independence and frightens families into thinking about care homes. A reversible cause changes the whole outlook.
Older people often buy sleep aids without seeing them as “medicines”. Pharmacists can flag anticholinergic products at the point of sale.

legal.t: Confusion does not remove capacity. Seek Harold’s consent for his daughter’s involvement and for the plan; assess capacity for specific decisions only if doubt arises (Mental Capacity Act 2005).

professional.t: Report suspected adverse drug reactions in older people via the MHRA Yellow Card scheme, and record the reaction on the record so the drug is not restarted.
NICE NG5: medicines reconciliation and structured review, including over-the-counter products, for older people on multiple medicines. Consider a practice pharmacist review.

community.t: Ask his usual pharmacy to note that sedating antihistamines should be avoided for him; community pharmacists can support deprescribing.

redFlags: Unable to pass urine with lower abdominal pain or swelling — acute retention, same-day catheterisation
Fluctuating confusion, drowsiness or fever — delirium (NICE CG103), look for infection and retention
Falls, new urinary incontinence or rising creatinine — obstruction or wider harm from the drugs
psychosocial: Family fear of dementia and care homes
Harold’s embarrassment about the chemist sleeping tablet
Impact on his independence and daily life
ice: Idea: “It’s his age, or he’s getting dementia”
Concern: “We’re losing him — it only goes one way”
Expectation: an explanation and perhaps a memory test

playbook.diagnosis: “The pattern — muddled thinking, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation and trouble passing urine, starting weeks after a new bladder tablet — is a side effect of a group of medicines he is taking three of. It is very likely to improve once they are reduced.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of these medicines as each turning down the same dial in the body. One on its own might be fine; three together turn it down so far that the bladder, the bowels and the brain all slow down. Turn them off, and the dial comes back up.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried this was the start of dementia — I can’t promise, but the speed and the timing point strongly to the medicines, and that’s something we can reverse.”
management.psychosocial: Thank Harold for disclosing the sleeping tablet; involve his daughter with his consent; give written instructions for the amitriptyline taper.
sharedPlan: Stop oxybutynin and the OTC sedating antihistamine; taper amitriptyline gradually (BNF), reviewing its purpose (NICE NG59)
Same-day face-to-face bladder examination and scan; U&E and delirium bloods
Bladder training for urgency; non-anticholinergic drug only if needed (NICE CG97, TA290 with BP check)
safetyNet: Cannot pass urine, or painful swollen abdomen — A&E
Very drowsy, feverish or suddenly more confused — same-day contact; review in about two weeks to reassess thinking

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you spot a reversible cause hiding behind the word “dementia”. It is failed by accepting the family’s framing, adding drugs, or missing the bladder.

items.fail: Referring to the memory clinic without reviewing the medicines.
items.why: NICE NG97 asks clinicians to consider anticholinergic burden before referring suspected dementia. Missing a reversible cause is unsafe.
items.fix: Link the timeline to the new drug, reduce the burden, and reassess thinking in about two weeks.

items.fail: Never asking about medicines from the chemist.
items.why: The sedating antihistamine is the hidden third drug; without it the review is incomplete.
items.fix: “Anything you buy yourself — for sleep, colds, allergies?”

items.fail: Treating the urinary symptoms on video without an examination.
items.why: Retention cannot be excluded remotely. A full bladder needs same-day assessment and possibly a catheter.
items.fix: Arrange same-day face-to-face examination, bladder scan and U&E; give clear A&E advice.

items.fail: Stopping amitriptyline abruptly along with everything else.
items.why: The BNF advises gradual withdrawal of tricyclics to avoid withdrawal effects.
items.fix: Stop oxybutynin and the antihistamine now; taper amitriptyline with a written plan.

items.why: Harold is the patient and is able to take part. Speaking over him fails Relating to Others.
items.fix: Ask his consent for her presence, and direct questions and decisions to him.

items.fail: Hearing “is it dementia?” and replying “don’t worry” without explanation.
items.why: Empty reassurance does not address the fear; a reasoned, honest reframe does.
items.fix: Explain why the speed and timing point to the medicines, and promise a proper recheck if concern remains.

items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “A group of medicines that dry things up and slow the bladder, bowels and brain.”

wordPics.fail: Accepts “it’s his age” or refers to the memory clinic; adds laxatives or another bladder drug; never asks about chemist medicines; misses the retention.
wordPics.pass: Links the symptoms to the new drug, finds the OTC antihistamine, stops the oxybutynin, plans a bladder check and reviews after withdrawal.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains the anticholinergic effect in plain words; gives the hopeful reframe while being honest about uncertainty; tapers amitriptyline safely; arranges same-day face-to-face assessment of retention; plans a non-anticholinergic route for the urgency; the family leave relieved and clear.

avoid.dont: “At 78, some memory decline is expected — let’s refer to the memory clinic.”
avoid.instead: “This came on over weeks after a new tablet — that points to the medicine, and it’s likely to reverse.”
avoid.why: Labelling dementia before removing a reversible cause is a Tasks fail (NICE NG97).

avoid.dont: “Let’s add a laxative for the constipation and switch to a different bladder tablet.”
avoid.instead: “The fix is taking tablets away, not adding more.”
avoid.why: Treating side effects with more drugs is the prescribing cascade.

avoid.dont: “Why didn’t you tell us you were taking sleeping tablets?”
avoid.instead: “I’m really glad you mentioned it — lots of people don’t realise those count.”
avoid.why: Judgement stops disclosure; gratitude keeps the review honest.

Here’s what I suggest. Stop the oxybutynin today, and stop the chemist sleeping tablet. The amitriptyline needs to come down gradually rather than stopping suddenly — I’ll give you a simple plan. Does that sound all right to you, Mr Inglis?
SCA_MODELS.why: Deprescribing plan with safe amitriptyline withdrawal, agreed with the patient

SCA_MODELS.text: (Harold) Yes. I want my head back.

There’s one thing I can’t do on video: feel your bladder. Because it feels full and you’re only dribbling, I want you seen in person today for an examination and a bladder scan, and some blood tests including your kidneys. If your bladder is holding a lot, you may need a catheter for a while to let it recover.
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges same-day face-to-face retention assessment and bloods

SCA_MODELS.text: (Daughter) I can bring him in this afternoon.

Thank you. For the urgency, once things settle, we’ll try bladder training first and look at other options that don’t affect thinking. For sleep and your back, we’ll find gentler approaches rather than more tablets. And I’ll report this reaction so it’s recorded.
SCA_MODELS.why: Plans safer alternatives and Yellow Card reporting

SCA_MODELS.text: (Harold) That’s a relief.

Before you come in — if you can’t pass any urine at all, or the tummy becomes painful and swollen, go straight to A&E. Same if you become very drowsy, feverish or suddenly much more confused. I’ll see you again in about two weeks to check your memory and thinking once these medicines are out. If there’s still a concern then, we’ll look into it properly.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific retention and delirium safety-net; planned cognitive reassessment

SCA_MODELS.text: (Daughter) Okay. That’s clear.
Could one of you tell me back which tablets are stopping and what happens this afternoon?
(Daughter) Stop the bladder tablet and the chemist sleeping one, cut the amitriptyline down slowly, come in this afternoon for the bladder check and bloods, and back in two weeks.
Perfect. You were right to bring him — the speed it came on was the clue, and it’s a fixable one.
SCA_MODELS.why: Affirms the family’s concern and closes warmly

SCA_STEM.name: Harold Inglis
pmh: Urinary urgency — oxybutynin started about 3 weeks ago
SCA_STEM.recent: Oxybutynin started for urinary urgency about three weeks ago. Amitriptyline on repeat for back pain.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment booked by his daughter: “Dad has become confused and constipated over the last few weeks.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG97 — Dementia (2018): medicines with anticholinergic burden · NICE CG97 — Lower urinary tract symptoms in men (2010, updated 2015)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: New confusion, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation and difficulty passing urine weeks after starting oxybutynin — on top of amitriptyline and a bought sedating antihistamine — is anticholinergic burden until proven otherwise. Reduce the burden, check for retention today, and reassess memory only once the drugs are out.

points.t: Anticholinergic effects: confusion and memory problems, drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, fast heart rate. Several drugs together add up; older people are most sensitive. Onset over weeks after a new drug points to the drug, not dementia.

Be aware that some commonly prescribed medicines add to anticholinergic burden and cause cognitive impairment. Consider minimising them, and look for alternatives, when assessing whether to refer someone with suspected dementia. Validated burden scales exist; NICE NG97 does not favour one.

Sedating antihistamines sold for sleep are anticholinergic and are often not on the GP record. A full medicine review includes over-the-counter and herbal products (NICE NG5, medicines optimisation, 2015).

Stop the oxybutynin and the bought antihistamine. Amitriptyline should be withdrawn gradually rather than stopped abruptly (BNF); NICE NG59 does not recommend tricyclics for low back pain, so review its purpose. STOPP/START (version 3, 2023, international) lists these combinations in older adults.

Anticholinergics can cause urinary retention — palpable bladder, pain, dribbling or overflow. Acute painful retention needs same-day catheterisation. Subacute confusion also needs a delirium check (NICE CG103): look for infection, constipation, retention, dehydration and check bloods including U&E.

For men with overactive bladder symptoms, NICE CG97 advises bladder training and assessment of the lower urinary tract (including residual volume) before drugs. If a drug is needed, mirabegron is an option (NICE TA290); it is contraindicated in severe uncontrolled hypertension, so check BP (MHRA Drug Safety Update, October 2015).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Sought Harold’s consent for his daughter to join; heard the full story and brought Harold in directly.
Impact on daily life, falls, the family’s fear of care homes, how he manages at home.
Followed “it came on quickly” and “opposite of what I went for”; picked up the hesitation before the OTC disclosure.
Idea (age or dementia); concern (losing him, care homes); expectation (an explanation and maybe a memory test).
Same-day face-to-face bladder examination and scan; U&E and delirium bloods; cognitive reassessment after withdrawal.
Anticholinergic burden versus delirium from infection or retention, versus a new dementia.
Acute urinary retention, delirium, renal impairment from obstruction.
Anticholinergic toxicity from stacked drugs (oxybutynin, amitriptyline, OTC antihistamine) with urinary retention.
Stop oxybutynin and antihistamine; taper amitriptyline (BNF); bladder training then non-anticholinergic option (NICE CG97, TA290).
Reviews why amitriptyline is prescribed (NICE NG59), sleep and back pain alternatives, constipation.
A&E for complete retention or pain; delirium symptoms named; review in about two weeks; Yellow Card report.

social.t: Sudden confusion threatens independence and frightens families into thinking about care homes. A reversible cause changes the whole outlook.
Older people often buy sleep aids without seeing them as “medicines”. Pharmacists can flag anticholinergic products at the point of sale.

legal.t: Confusion does not remove capacity. Seek Harold’s consent for his daughter’s involvement and for the plan; assess capacity for specific decisions only if doubt arises (Mental Capacity Act 2005).

professional.t: Report suspected adverse drug reactions in older people via the MHRA Yellow Card scheme, and record the reaction on the record so the drug is not restarted.
NICE NG5: medicines reconciliation and structured review, including over-the-counter products, for older people on multiple medicines. Consider a practice pharmacist review.

community.t: Ask his usual pharmacy to note that sedating antihistamines should be avoided for him; community pharmacists can support deprescribing.

redFlags: Unable to pass urine with lower abdominal pain or swelling — acute retention, same-day catheterisation
Fluctuating confusion, drowsiness or fever — delirium (NICE CG103), look for infection and retention
Falls, new urinary incontinence or rising creatinine — obstruction or wider harm from the drugs
psychosocial: Family fear of dementia and care homes
Harold’s embarrassment about the chemist sleeping tablet
Impact on his independence and daily life
ice: Idea: “It’s his age, or he’s getting dementia”
Concern: “We’re losing him — it only goes one way”
Expectation: an explanation and perhaps a memory test

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The pattern — muddled thinking, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation and trouble passing urine, starting weeks after a new bladder tablet — is a side effect of a group of medicines he is taking three of. It is very likely to improve once they are reduced.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of these medicines as each turning down the same dial in the body. One on its own might be fine; three together turn it down so far that the bladder, the bowels and the brain all slow down. Turn them off, and the dial comes back up.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried this was the start of dementia — I can’t promise, but the speed and the timing point strongly to the medicines, and that’s something we can reverse.”
management.psychosocial: Thank Harold for disclosing the sleeping tablet; involve his daughter with his consent; give written instructions for the amitriptyline taper.
sharedPlan: Stop oxybutynin and the OTC sedating antihistamine; taper amitriptyline gradually (BNF), reviewing its purpose (NICE NG59)
Same-day face-to-face bladder examination and scan; U&E and delirium bloods
Bladder training for urgency; non-anticholinergic drug only if needed (NICE CG97, TA290 with BP check)
safetyNet: Cannot pass urine, or painful swollen abdomen — A&E
Very drowsy, feverish or suddenly more confused — same-day contact; review in about two weeks to reassess thinking

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you spot a reversible cause hiding behind the word “dementia”. It is failed by accepting the family’s framing, adding drugs, or missing the bladder.

items.fail: Referring to the memory clinic without reviewing the medicines.
items.why: NICE NG97 asks clinicians to consider anticholinergic burden before referring suspected dementia. Missing a reversible cause is unsafe.
items.fix: Link the timeline to the new drug, reduce the burden, and reassess thinking in about two weeks.

items.fail: Never asking about medicines from the chemist.
items.why: The sedating antihistamine is the hidden third drug; without it the review is incomplete.
items.fix: “Anything you buy yourself — for sleep, colds, allergies?”

items.fail: Treating the urinary symptoms on video without an examination.
items.why: Retention cannot be excluded remotely. A full bladder needs same-day assessment and possibly a catheter.
items.fix: Arrange same-day face-to-face examination, bladder scan and U&E; give clear A&E advice.

items.fail: Stopping amitriptyline abruptly along with everything else.
items.why: The BNF advises gradual withdrawal of tricyclics to avoid withdrawal effects.
items.fix: Stop oxybutynin and the antihistamine now; taper amitriptyline with a written plan.

items.why: Harold is the patient and is able to take part. Speaking over him fails Relating to Others.
items.fix: Ask his consent for her presence, and direct questions and decisions to him.

items.fail: Hearing “is it dementia?” and replying “don’t worry” without explanation.
items.why: Empty reassurance does not address the fear; a reasoned, honest reframe does.
items.fix: Explain why the speed and timing point to the medicines, and promise a proper recheck if concern remains.

items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “A group of medicines that dry things up and slow the bladder, bowels and brain.”
